content: Distributed computing is a field of computer science that studies distributed systems. A distributed system is a system whose components are located on different networked computers, which communicate and coordinate their actions by passing messages to one another from any system. The components interact with one another in order to achieve a common goal. Three significant challenges of distributed systems are: maintaining concurrency of components, lack of a global clock, and permitting independent failure of components. When a component of one system fails, the entire system does not have to fail. Examples of distributed systems vary from SOA-based systems to massively multiplayer online games to peer-to-peer applications.

Information retrieval (IR) is the science of searching for information in a document, searching for documents themselves, and also searching for the metadata that describes data, and for databases of texts, images or sounds. Automated information retrieval systems are used to reduce what has been called information overload. A search engine is an information retrieval software system designed to help find information stored on a computer system. The search results are generally presented in a list and are commonly called hits. Web search engines work by storing information about many web pages, which they retrieve from the HTML markup itself. These pages are retrieved by a Web crawler.

In information retrieval, Okapi BM25 (BM is an abbreviation of best matching) is a ranking function used by search engines to estimate the relevance of documents to a given search query. It is based on the probabilistic relevance framework developed in the 1970s and 1980s by Stephen E. Robertson, Karen Sparck Jones, and others. The name of the actual ranking function is BM25. The BM25 function scores a document based on the query terms appearing in that document, regardless of the inter-relationship between query terms. It penalizes longer documents to account for document length bias and uses a saturation function for term frequency.

An inverted index is an index data structure storing a mapping from content, such as words or numbers, to its locations in a document or a set of documents. In computer science, an inverted index is the central component of a search engine indexing algorithm. A search engine indexes documents by mapping each unique word to the list of documents that contain it. These document lists are commonly referred to as posting lists. Each entry in a posting list is called a posting, which typically records the document identifier and the term frequency within that document.

Replication is the process of sharing information so as to ensure consistency between redundant resources, such as software or hardware components, to improve reliability, fault-tolerance, or accessibility. In database systems, primary-replica replication designates one node as the primary to handle write operations while replicas synchronize state asynchronously or synchronously. Write-ahead logging (WAL) is a family of techniques for providing atomicity and durability in database systems. In a system using WAL, all modifications are written to a log before they are applied to the primary database file.

Fault tolerance is the property that enables a system to continue operating properly in the event of the failure of some of its components. If its operating quality decreases at all, the decrease is proportional to the severity of the failure. Incremental recovery allows a failed or lagging node to catch up by replaying only the missed log entries rather than rebuilding its entire state from scratch. Checkpointing periodically bounds log retention and speeds up recovery.

The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is one of the main protocols of the Internet protocol suite. It originated in the initial network implementation in which it complemented the Internet Protocol (IP). Therefore, the entire suite is commonly referred to as TCP/IP. TCP provides reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of a stream of octets between applications running on hosts communicating via an IP network. Major internet applications such as the World Wide Web, email, and file transfer rely on TCP.

An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware, software resources, and provides common services for computer programs. Virtual memory is a memory management technique that provides an idealized abstraction of the storage resources that are actually available on a given machine which creates the illusion to users of a very large memory. The operating system maps virtual addresses used by an application into physical addresses in computer memory.

Concurrency is the execution of multiple instruction sequences at the same time. It happens in the operating system when there are several process threads running in parallel. The running threads can interact with each other through shared memory or message passing. Synchronization is required to avoid race conditions, deadlocks, and resource starvation. Mutexes, semaphores, and atomic operations are standard synchronization primitives used in modern concurrent software architectures.

In mathematics and computer science, an algorithm is a finite sequence of rigorous instructions, typically used to solve a class of specific problems or to perform a computation. Computational complexity theory is a subfield of computer science that focuses on classifying computational problems according to their resource usage, and relating these classes to each other. The most common resources considered are time (the number of steps needed) and space (the amount of memory needed).
